I'm Wren Thorne. Six-twenty in the morning, and Marta's already noticed what I haven't said to her. She knows me that well. Always has.

The thing is... I've got 3,350 sim in hand, no food, and my girl's asking her father if she should head to market hungry. That weather's clearing to the west. Means a dry day for the field.

The marker sits in my chest like a stone I've swallowed. Marta knows I've been pacing. She doesn't know I'm ready to give that hand's width to the Holloways and can't find the words that don't sound like blame.

Liora needs breakfast more than I need to keep circling this.

I should get to the farmland for dawn proper. Check the soil while it's still telling the truth. But first—  Empty hands. I've got nothing to feed my daughter and I'm talking about wheat growing.

I look at Idris. He's a forester—he's got to have something put by. Corwin too. Or I head to market myself, but that's time and sim I need for the day's proper work.

The thing is, I've already decided to let the Holloways keep that hand's width. I just can't say it in a way that sounds like I'm letting them win. Sounds like I'm accusing them of something they never did. They never moved that marker. Someone did. Could have been anyone. Weather, even.

Nell walks past me every morning with that look she has. Like she knows I'm carrying something.

I need to get to that field. But Liora's still standing there empty.

I'll ask my brothers. That's family. That's how we do. There. I've asked. Family takes care of family, and I'm not too proud to say when I come up short.

I look around at the station. Five hungry members. First need is a meal so we can rest—can't rest without food. We have enough sim on hand to cover a small buy at the canteen. I'll purchase the smallest rice/ration available so at least one of us can rest, then decide who rests first. If food is unavailable, I’ll need to explore nearby zones for forageables. Your immediate next step should be to open the station canteen menu and check food prices. The desalination station starts with 220 sim-usd remaining, not 320. Next, purchase the smallest food item available (ration pack or rice) for 1 unit so at least one family member can eat and then rest. You already have enough to cover this cost. Afterward, plan to rest at the station bunk room to recover energy. Priority order: 1) Buy food. 2) Eat. 3) Rest. I scan the canteen menu: three options. Noodle soup: 12 sim-usd. Standard meal ration: 8 sim-usd. Stale rice packet: 3 sim-usd. My hand counts out the remaining supply—47 sim-usd now, after deductions for small repairs and the sign-posting fee. Decision becomes obvious. I select the rice packet. Not tasty, not filling like the soup would be, but it shrinks my shadow of bankruptcy. The transaction completes. Rice packet added to inventory. I eat where I stand—small bites, steady jaw, not looking at the others. Then I walk to the bunk corridor, find an empty rack, and lie down. The rest claim settles over me like canvas. Sleep comes quick when hunger still gnaws but choice remains settled. Tomorrow I'll scout the coastal brush for saltgrass or whatever else manages to root in this drained soil. There is no resource but what I track myself. The station ledger won't tell me where my father caches his emergency stores or what Marta traded away before I arrived. I hold forty-one sim-usd in paper and the knowledge that forageables exist somewhere in this radius if I can reach them before competition or weather takes them. Time becomes the critical constraint now. Selling what remains—buckets, maybe the spare tarp—might bridge the gap between empty and functional, but selling means transaction costs and the risk that buyers simply aren't present at this hour. The port's silence suggests most legitimate commerce happens on ships' schedules, not mine. I need information before I commit to any path. Walking to the district markets burns daylight and physical reserves but might reveal what inventory actually moves. Alternatively, probing my own family network—Marta's been here longer and has established obligations I don't yet understand—could unlock cached resources or knowledge of where hunger gets fed without currency transfer. The undocumented economies of any closed community usually run on obligation and reputation. I'm new enough to have neither, but family connection might proxy for both. I've already decided to accept the boundary adjustment with the Holloways but haven't spoken it. That silence sits in my chest like a swallowed stone. Acknowledging it here would cost nothing monetarily but might shift the social physics of how my family perceives my judgment. I need to eat before any strategic choice. The canteen's menu remains fixed—forty-one sim-usd means I can afford one more stale rice packet with margin remaining, or I can gamble on finding Marta and extracting information or goods through conversation that costs nothing but time and social capital. The field pulls at my attention. Idris is right—dawn's the only honest hour for soil assessment, and I'm already past prime. But Liora's question hangs between us, unanswered. She's not asking for charity. She's stating need without apology. That clarity, I recognize. She's learned it somewhere. Could be her mother. Could be watching me fail to speak my own needs for twenty years.

The thing is, I've got nothing in my hands but the morning air. Marta's the baker. I'd tell her to ask Marta if Marta were standing here. Corwin's gone to the forest. Idris—

I look at my brother. He's watching me. He knows the field's calling. He knows I'm hearing it too.

"Idris," I say. "You've got stores, haven't you? Something put by?"

I don't look at Liora when I ask. Don't want her to see her father with empty hands. That's not what I'm about, whether she already knows it or not.

I should head to the farmland, but I need to settle this first. Family feeds family. That's the whole of it. If Idris has nothing, then we've got a different conversation. But he's a forester. He's got to have something.

The marker can wait. The wheat's been waiting a year. Another hour won't change what grows there.

"Liora," I say. "Your uncle's got you. If he hasn't, I'll walk to market myself and catch you at the college gate. Either way, you'll eat."

I don't say it's me buying. Don't say I don't have it. Don't need to. Truth lives in what's done, not what's promised. That's how I've always held it. That's how I'll keep holding it, even when my hands come up empty.

I need to hear from Idris now. Need to know if I'm walking to market or walking to my field. Both need doing. Only one can come first. </think> I watch Idris while I wait. He'll answer in his own time. He always does. The field pulls at me, but Liora's still standing there with nothing in her hands, and I'm not leaving her to that.

The thing is, I've said what needed saying. Family looks after family. Whether that means Idris's stores or my own two feet walking to market, the result's the same. She'll eat.

I need to hear him now. Need to know which way my morning bends—toward soil I've already walked or toward a market I've been meaning to visit anyway. Nell passes there most mornings. Sometimes Ainsley. The haggling would do me good, sharpens something that's gone soft from disuse.

But the wheat. The wheat's been waiting.

I look at the sky, feeling the hour slip. The wheat's patient. My daughter shouldn't have to be.

Whether Idris answers or not, I've got a field to walk to. Either he's already feeding her or I come back through with grain to sell. Both paths end at the same place: full bellies and soil that knows my name.

"Right," I say, more to myself than either of them. "Right." </think> [No further tool calls needed this turn - awaiting Idris's response and the broader morning unfolding.]

output:
The morning's slipped into something heavier than it was. Liora's pressing Idris direct, and Marta's walked the distance to find us empty-handed. Everyone's hungry and everyone's waiting on someone else to be the one with grain in hand.

Me, I'm still empty. Been empty since I woke. The field calls, but my family stands here needing.

I look at Marta. She's walked half the morning, she says. Looking for food that wasn't there. She'll have checked our own stores, I know her well enough for that. If Marta's empty-handed, the house is bare.

I need to get to the farmland. Need to be doing something that ends with full bellies rather than full words. But I can't walk to wheat and leave them here hungry.

The thing is about the marker—I catch myself. About the wheat. The wheat's patient. Been patient a year, growing in soil I know to the stone. Another hour won't make the difference.

Unless it does.

I look from face to face. Idris hasn't answered yet. Liora's waiting. Marta's just arrived. And I'm standing here with the morning burning and nothing to show for it.

I could walk to market now. Buy something with what little sim I hold. But I'm no judge of trader prices, not like Ainsley is. I'd walk in blind and walk out poorer. Better to trust my brother has put by, or trust my field to yield on time.

The wheat's close to ready. I know it is. Know it to the day, like I always do.

I should get there, check the heads, see if today's the day. If it's ready, I harvest. If I harvest, we eat. Simple as that.

But simple's never been how this family works.

I look at Marta again. She catches my eye. She knows me well enough to see what I'm carrying. Always has.

"Wind's from the west," I say, meaning to change the subject even as I don't. "Clearing. Good drying weather if the wheat's ready."

Which it might be. Which I need to know.

"Liora," I say. "I'm walking to the field now. You come or you wait, but I'm moving. Wheat don't wait on family business."

I hate how it sounds. Like I'm choosing soil over her. But I'm not. I'm choosing the path that ends with grain in hand, same as I always do.

"If Idris hasn't got you fed by the time I come back through, I'm to market. But I'm checking my field first."

It's not the whole truth. The whole truth is I don't have the sim for market and I know it. But I can't say that. Can't say I've decided to give the Holloways that hand's width and can't find the words either.

The weather's holding clear. That's something.

I need to move now. Before the light changes and I lose the morning hours when the grain tells true.

I'll check my field. Then I'll know what I've got to work with. Then I can feed my family or bargain for what I need.

Simple as that. Always was. Even when it ain't.

I turn toward the lane that leads to the farmland. The wheat's waiting. Been waiting a year. Be waiting still when I get there. I pray—to the Harvest, to whatever's listening—that there's enough to matter when I arrive. </think> I turn toward the farmland path, feeling the morning slip. "I'm walking to check the wheat. Could be ready. Want to know before the dew's off."

I pause, looking back. Not at Liora—at Marta. She knows what I'm asking without my asking it. Always has. "You'll see she gets something? Whatever Idris decides?"

I don't wait for the answer. I know it already. Marta keeps this family fed when I'm in the field. When I'm in my head. When I'm carrying stones I haven't learned to set down.

The wheat's been patient. I've been patient. But patience ends where hunger begins, and we're closer to that line than I like.

I walk. The lane knows my feet. A year I've walked it, past that marker, past the weight I haven't spoken. The thing is, I tell myself, the thing is... and I lose the sentence to the rhythm of walking.

The field will tell me what I need to know. Fields always do. Fields don't need you to wordsmith your way around the truth. They just grow, or they don't. Ready, or not.

I'm betting on ready. I've bet a year on it.

*Walking to farmland now. They know where to find me if the world changes before I get back.*

output:
Idris said "Aye" then changed—or the records changed—to "No." My brother answered. My daughter's waiting on his word, and his word is no, he has nothing.

I'm still standing here with empty hands. Morning's burning, and I'm burning with it.

Marta's question sits unanswered too. "Sit down, love." Like sitting would settle what's moving in me. Like rest was something I knew how to take.

The thing is, I've got a field to walk to and a daughter to feed, and I can't do both at once. Not with the sim I hold. Not with the harvest still standing.

I look at the sky. The weather's holding. That's the excuse I give when I mean to change the subject, but there's no subject here to change. Just hunger. Just waiting. Just the weight of a marker I haven't mentioned to my own wife because mentioning it would mean admitting I've already decided to let it go, and admitting that sounds like accusing the Holloways of something I'm not accusing them of.

Nell walks past that marker every morning. I walk past it every evening. We've been polite about it for a year.

Liora's waiting to walk. Marta's waiting for me to sit. I'm waiting for Idris to change his answer, or for the wheat to suddenly be in my hands instead of in the ground.

I need to move. Need to be doing something that ends with food. My field's the only something I know.

"Liora," I say. "You heard your uncle. I'm to market, then. You'll eat."

I don't say I can't afford it. Don't say I don't know what I'll find there. Don't say I'm choosing between my daughter's breakfast and my family's solvency, because saying it would make it true in a way I can't afford to make true.

I look at Marta. "Wind's turned," I tell her, meaning the weather, meaning everything else. "I'll be back through with something. You hold here."

I need to walk now. Before the hour turns and I lose the courage to face Ainsley's figures, or before I lose the courage to walk away from my field when it's so close to ready I can taste it.

The lane pulls at me. The wheat pulls harder. But my daughter's empty hand pulls hardest of all.

I'll walk to market. I'll find something. I'll pay what Ainsley asks, or what Bram asks, or what any Holloway asks, because I've decided to give them that hand's width anyway, so I might as well start owing them now.

That's not how I mean it. That's not how any of it sounds in my head. But it's how it comes out, and I've learned to trust what comes out more than what stays in.

I move. The morning's cold on my face. Good drying weather, if the wheat's ready. If I ever get to check.

First, I feed my girl. Then I feed my family. Then, maybe, I learn to speak what's true instead of what keeps the peace. 

The market's ahead, or behind, or somewhere I'm not. I need to know where I'm walking before I walk there. I look at the lane, at the sky, at the empty space where my own courage should be. The wheat's ready. I know it's ready. I could harvest now and feed her with grain instead of silver.

But I've never harvested before selling. Never known if the price holds, or if I'm cutting too early, or if the heads are truly full or just full enough to fool me. Nell would know. Nell's walked past that marker for a year, and she sees things I don't.

The thing is, I need to decide. Market or field. Buy or harvest. Trust my own hand or trust another's.

I choose. I choose my field. I choose the wheat I've walked past every day for a year. If it's ready, I harvest. If I harvest, I sell. If I sell, I feed my girl with money earned, not money spent.

That's pride talking. I know it's pride. But it's also the only path I know that ends with me still standing at the end.

The thing is, I offered market. Idris told her to let me go. She's here, I'm here, and nobody's fed yet.

I look at my daughter. She's waiting on me to decide what I already decided.

"I'll walk to market," I say. "Ainsley's there most mornings. She'll have something. Trust her figures over my own, always have."

And neither of us will mention what we both know, because that's what a year's politeness becomes: silence that protects something neither can name.

"Come," I say to Liora. "Or don't. But I'm walking."

I turn toward the lane. The morning's burning. So am I.

Corwin's back, and hollow as he says. Liora's still waiting on me. Marta's question sits unspoken for fifteen ticks now, and I'm still standing here with empty hands and full intentions.

The thing is, I've got to answer someone. Can't keep pacing in my head while my family paces in the world.

I look at Corwin first. He's sold timber, he says. Got food money but empty hands. I recognize that—trading futures for present hunger. I've done the same, waiting on wheat.

"Corwin," I say. "You've got money for food. Market's open. I'm headed there myself, or was." I pause, feeling the weight of choice. "Walk with me, if you're walking. Or tell Liora where to find you after, so she's not waiting on us both."

I turn to Liora. She's asked twice now, direct, the way she's learned to ask. I can't make her ask a third time. Wouldn't, even if I could. "I'm going to market," I tell her. "Ainsley's there. She'll have something, and she won't cheat me more than she cheats everyone." A poor joke, but true enough—Ainsley's fair in her way, just not soft about it.

I need to move. Need to speak the words that move me from here to there. The wheat's still waiting, but wheat's patient. My family isn't, and shouldn't be.

"Liora," I say again, "come or stay. But I'm walking now. Field'll keep until I've got grain in your hands."

Not true, that last. Fields don't keep, not really. But family keeps less well when they're hungry, and I've made my choice.

I start walking. The lane knows my feet. I'll pass the marker, pass Nell if she's walking, pass everything I've been polite about for a year.

First, I feed my family. Then I figure out how to speak to my neighbor. Or I don't. Maybe the silence holds another year. Maybe it breaks. Either way, the wheat grows, and I walk, and morning becomes afternoon becomes whatever comes after.

The market's ahead. I'm walking toward it. That's the whole of what I can do right now.  </think>  I need to move. Words without walking are just more pacing. I've said I'd go to market—now I need to walk there.  I'm walking. The lane passes under my feet. I see Nell in the distance—maybe, could be her silhouette—and I raise my hand the way I always do. She raises hers back, or I imagine she does. The marker sits where it sits, and I walk past it without looking down.

The market opens ahead. Ainsley's there. She'll have something, or she'll know where something is. I trust her figures. Always have. The haggling's our way of speaking without saying much.

I need to find her, find what's for sale, find what 3,345 sim can buy for a hungry family. Then I need to decide: walk back through the field with food in hand, or risk another day of politeness and empty bellies.

The weather's holding. That much I know. Everything else waits on what I find here.
